smitt: Fine clay or ocher made up into balls, used for marking sheep. [Eng.] Woodsward.
smartness: The quality or state of being smart.
smooth: 1. Having an even surface, or a surface so even that no roughness or points can be perceived by the touch; not rough; as, smooth glass; smooth porcelain. Chaucer. | Smoothly. Chaucer. Smooth runs the water where the brook is deep. Shak.
smirch: To smear with something which stains, or makes dirty; to smutch; to begrime; to soil; to sully. I'll . . . with a kind of umber smirch my face. Shak.
smash: To break in pieces by violence; to dash to pieces; to crush. Here everything is broken and smashed to pieces. Burke. | To break up, or to pieces suddenly, as the result of collision or pressure.
smartweed: An acrid plant of the genus Polygonum (P. Hydropiper), which produces smarting if applied where the skin is tender.
smuggle: 1. To import or export secretly, contrary to the law; to import or export without paying the duties imposed by law; as, to smuggle lace. 2. Fig.: To convey or introduce clandestinely. | To import or export in violation of the customs laws.
smicker: To look amorously or wantonly; to smirk. | Amorous; wanton; gay; spruce. (old)
smallsword: A light sword used for thrusting only; especially, the sword worn by civilians of rank in the eighteenth century.
smuggler: 1. One who smuggles. 2. A vessel employed in smuggling.
smoke: 1. The visible exhalation, vapor, or substance that escapes, or expelled, from a burning body, especially from burning vegetable matter, as wood, coal, peat, or the like. | 1. To emit smoke; to throw off volatile matter in the form of vapor or exhalation; to reek. Hard by a cottage chimney smokes. Milton. 2. Hence, to burn; to be kindled; to rage.
smeller: 1. One who smells, or perceives by the sense of smell; one who gives out smell. 2. The nose. [Pugilists' Slang]
smart: 1. To feel a lively, pungent local pain; -- said of some part of the body as the seat of irritation; as, my finger smarts; these wounds smart. Chaucer. Shak. 2. To feel a pungent pain of mind; | To cause a smart in. "A goad that . . . smarts the flesh." T. Adams.
smeir: A salt glaze on pottery, made by adding common salt to an earthenware glaze.
smoothchinned: Having a smooth chin; beardless. Drayton.
smatter: 1. To talk superficially or ignorantly; to babble; to chatter. Of state affairs you can not smatter. Swift. 2. To have a slight taste, or a slight, superficial knowledge, of anything; to smack. | 1. To talk superficially about. 2. To gain a slight taste of; to acquire a slight, superficial knowledge of; to smack. Chaucer.
smarten: To make smart or spruce; -- usually with up. [Colloq.] She had to go and smarten herself up somewhat. W. Black.
smoother: One who, or that which, smooths.
smoothbore: Having a bore of perfectly smooth surface; -- distinguished from rifled. -- n. A smoothbore firearm.
smudge: 1. A suffocating smoke. Grose. 2. A heap of damp combustibles partially ignited and burning slowly, placed on the windward side of a house, tent, or the like, in order, by the thick smoke, to keep… | 1. To stifle or smother with smoke; to smoke by means of a smudge. 2. To smear; to smutch; to soil; to blacken with smoke.
smerky: Smart; jaunty; spruce. See Smirk, a. (old) So smerk, so smooth, his pricked ears. Spenser.
smorzando: Growing gradually fainter and softer; dying away; morendo.
smit: imp. & p. p. of Smite. Spenser. Smit with the beauty of so fair a scene. Cowper. | 3d. pers. sing. pres. of Smite. Chaucer.
smee: (a) The pintail duck. (b) The widgeon. (c) The poachard. (d) The smew. [Prov. Eng.]
smew: (a) small European merganser (Mergus albellus) which has a white crest; -- called also smee, smee duck, white merganser, and white nun. (b) The hooded merganser. [Local, U.S.]
smithsonian: Of or pertaining to the Englishman J.L.M. Smithson, or to the national institution of learning which he endowed at Washington, D.C.; as, the Smithsonian Institution; Smithsonian Reports. -- n. The Smithsonian Institution.
smock: 1. A woman's under-garment; a shift; a chemise. In her smock, with head and foot all bare. Chaucer. 2. A blouse; a smoock frock. Carlyle. | Of or pertaining to a smock; resembling a smock; hence, of or pertaining to a woman. Smock mill, a windmill of which only the cap turns round to meet the wind, in distinction from a post mill, whose…
smegma: The matter secreted by any of the sebaceous glands. Specifically: (a) The soapy substance covering the skin of newborn infants. (b) The cheesy, sebaceous matter which collects between the glans penis and the foreskin.
smear: 1. To overspread with anything unctuous, viscous, or adhesive; to daub; as, to smear anything with oil. "Smear the sleepy grooms with blood." Shak. 2. To soil in any way; to contaminate; to pollute; | 1. A fat, oily substance; oinment. Johnson. 2. Hence, a spot made by, or as by, an unctuous or adhesive substance; a blot or blotch; a daub; a stain. Slow broke the morn, All damp and rolling vapor,…
smelting: a. & n. from Smelt. Smelting furnace (Metal.), a furnace in which ores are smelted or reduced.
smallness: The quality or state of being small.
smack: A small sailing vessel, commonly rigged as a sloop, used chiefly in the coasting and fishing trade. | 1. Taste or flavor, esp. a slight taste or flavor; savor; tincture; as, a smack of bitter in the medicine. Also used figuratively. So quickly they have taken a smack in covetousness.
smith: 1. One who forgess with the hammer; one who works in metals; as, a blacksmith, goldsmith, silversmith, and the like. Piers Plowman. Nor yet the smith hath learned to form a sword. Tate. 2. | To beat into shape; to fprge. (old) Chaucer. What smith that any [weapon] smitheth. Piers Plowman.
smaltine: A tin-white or gray mineral of metallic luster. It is an arsenide of cobalt, nickel, and iron. Called also speiskobalt.
smickering: Amorous glance or inclination. (old) "A smickering to our young lady." Dryden.
smoker: 1. One who dries or preserves by smoke. 2. One who smokes tobacco or the like. 3. A smoking car or compartment. [U. S.]
smouldering: Being in a state of suppressed activity; quiet but not dead. Some evil chance Will make the smoldering scandal break and blaze. Tennyson.
smilet: A little smile. Those happy smilets That played on her ripe lip. Shak.
smittlish: Infectious; catching. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.] H. Kingsley.
smorsato: Growing gradually fainter and softer; dying away; morendo.
smaragdine: Of or pertaining to emerald; resembling emerald; of an emerald green.
smatterer: One who has only a slight, superficial knowledge; a sciolist.
smut: 1. Foul matter, like soot or coal dust; also, a spot or soil made by such matter. 2. (Mining) Bad, soft coal, containing much earthy matter, found in the immediate locality of faults. 3. | 1. To stain or mark with smut; to blacken with coal, soot, or other dirty substance. 2. To taint with mildew, as grain. Bacon. 3. To blacken; to sully or taint; to tarnish. 4. To clear of smut;
smyrniot: Of or pertaining to Smyrna. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Smyrna.
smile: 1. To express amusement, pleasure, moderate joy, or love and kindness, by the features of the face; to laugh silently. He doth nothing but frown . . . He hears merry tales and smiles not. Shak. | 1. To express by a smile; as, to smile consent; to smile a welcome to visitors. 2. To affect in a certain way with a smile. And sharply smile prevailing folly dead. Young.
smoldering: Being in a state of suppressed activity; quiet but not dead. Some evil chance Will make the smoldering scandal break and blaze. Tennyson.
smaragdite: A green foliated kind of amphibole, observed in eclogite and some varietis of gabbro.
smoulder: 1. To burn and smoke without flame; to waste away by a slow and supressed combustion. The smoldering dust did round about him smoke. Spenser. 2. To exist in a state of suppressed or smothered… | To smother; to suffocate; to choke. (old) Holinshed. Palsgrave.
smokestack: A chimney; esp., a pipe serving as a chimney, as the pipe which carries off the smoke of a locomotive, the funnel of a steam vessel, etc.
smicket: A woman's under-garment; a smock. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Johnson.
smoothing: fr. Smooth, v. Smoothing iron, an iron instrument with a polished face, for smoothing clothes; a sadiron; a flatiron. -- Smoothing plane, a short, finely set plane, for smoothing and finishing work.
smell: 1. To perceive by the olfactory nerves, or organs of smell; to have a sensation of, excited through the nasal organs when affected by the appropriate materials or qualities; to obtain the scent of; | 1. small: 1. Having little size, compared with other things of the same kind; little in quantity or degree; diminutive; not large or extended in dimension; not great; not much; inconsiderable; as, a small man; | 1. In or to small extent, quantity, or degree; little; slightly. (old) "I wept but small." Chaucer. "It small avails my mood." Shak. 2. Not loudly; faintly; timidly. [Obs.
smug: Studiously neat or nice, especially in dress; spruce; affectedly precise; smooth and prim. They be so smug and smooth. Robynson (More's Utopia). The smug and scanty draperies of his style. | To make smug, or spruce. (old) Thus said, he smugged his beard, and stroked up fair. Dryton.
smirk: To smile in an affected or conceited manner; to smile with affected complaisance; to simper. | A forced or affected smile; a simper. The bride, all smirk and blush, had just entered. Sir W. Scott.
smallage: A biennial umbelliferous plant (Apium graveolens) native of the seacoats of Europe and Asia. When deprived of its acrid and even poisonous properties by cultivation, it becomes celery.
smattering: A slight, superficial knowledge of something; sciolism. I had a great desire, not able to attain to a superficial skill in any, to have some smattering in all. Burton.
smally: In a small quantity or degree; with minuteness. Ascham.
smeeth: To smoke; to blacken with smoke; to rub with soot. (old) | To smooth. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
smokehouse: A building where meat or fish is cured by subjecting it to a dense smoke.
smokedry: To dry by or in smoke.
smokelesspowder: A high-explosive gunpowder whose explosion produces little, if any, smoke.
smokable: Capable of being smoked; suitable or ready to be smoked; as, smokable tobacco.
smouch: To kiss closely. (old) P. Stubbes. | To smutch; to soil; as, to smouch the face.
smalt: A deep blue pigment or coloring material used in various arts. It is a vitreous substance made of cobalt, potash, and calcined quartz fused, and reduced to a powder.
smilax: (a) A genus of perennial climbing plants, usually with a prickly woody stem; green brier, or cat brier. The rootstocks of certain species are the source of the medicine called sarsaparilla. (b) A delicate trailing plant (Myrsiphyllum asparagoides) much used for decoration. It is a native of the Cape of Good Hope.
smiter: One who smites. I give my back to the smiters. Isa. l. 6.
smockfaced: Having a feminine countenance or complexion; smooth-faced; girlish. Fenton.
smallclothes: A man's garment for the hips and thighs; breeches. See Breeches.
smote: imp. (and rare p. p.) of Smite.
smaltite: A tin-white or gray mineral of metallic luster. It is an arsenide of cobalt, nickel, and iron. Called also speiskobalt.
smolder: 1. To burn and smoke without flame; to waste away by a slow and supressed combustion. The smoldering dust did round about him smoke. Spenser. 2. To exist in a state of suppressed or smothered… | To smother; to suffocate; to choke. (old) Holinshed. Palsgrave.
smotheredmate: Checkmate given when movement of the king is completely obstructed by his own men.
smoky: 1. Emitting smoke, esp. in large quantities or in an offensive manner; fumid; as, smoky fires. 2. Having the appearance or nature of smoke; as, a smoky fog. "Unlustrous as the smoky light." Shak. 3. Filled with smoke, or with a vapor resembling smoke; thick; as, a smoky atmosphere. 4. Subject to be filled with smoke from chimneys or fireplace; as, a smoky house. 5.
smokiness: The quality or state of being smoky.
smolt: A young salmon two or three years old, when it has acquired its silvery color.
smithing: The act or art of working or forging metals, as iron, into any desired shape. Moxon.
smugness: The quality or state of being smug.
smithcraft: The art or occupation of a smith; smithing. Sir W. Raleigh.
sminthurid: Any one of numerous small species of springtails, of the family Sminthurid, -- usually found on flowers. See Illust. under Collembola.
smacking: A sharp, quick noise; a smack. Like the faint smacking of an after kiss. Dryden. | Making a sharp, brisk sound; hence, brisk; as, a smacking breeze.
smoothtongued: Having a smooth tongue; plausible; flattering.
smilodon: An extinct genus of saber-toothed tigers. See Mach.
smectite: A hydrous silicate of alumina, of a greenish color, which, in certain states of humidity, appears transparent and almost gelatinous.
smutch: A stain; a dirty spot. B. Jonson. | To blacken with smoke, soot, or coal. [Written also smooch.] B. Jonson.
smither: 1. Light, fine rain. [Prov. Eng.] 2. pl. Fragments; atoms; finders. [Prov. Eng.] Smash the bottle to smithers. Tennyson.
smegmatic: Being of the nature of soap; soapy; cleansing; detersive.
smoothness: Quality or state of being smooth.
smokejack: A contrivance for turning a spit by means of a fly or wheel moved by the current of ascending air in a chimney.
smittle: Infection. [Pov. Eng.] Wright. | Infectious; catching. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.] H. Kingsley.
smeltery: A house or place for smelting.
smouldry: Smoldering; suffocating; smothery. (old) A flaming fire ymixt with smoldry smoke. Spenser.
smudginess: The quality or state of being smudged, soiled, or blurred. C. A. Young.
smockfrock: A coarse frock, or shirt, worn over the other dress, as by farm laborers. Macaulay.
smoor: To suffocate or smother. [Written also smore.] [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Sir T. More. Burns.
smilingness: Quality or state of being smiling. And made despair a smilingness assume. Byron.
smore: To smother. See Smoor. (old) Some dying vomit blood, and some were smored. Du Bartas.
smallpox: A contagious, constitutional, febrile disease characterized by a peculiar eruption; variola. The cutaneous eruption is at first a collection of papules which become vesicles (first flat, subsequently umbilicated) and then pustules, and finally thick crusts which slough after a certain time, often leaving a pit, or scar.
smithsonite: Native zinc carbonate. It generally occurs in stalactitic, reniform, or botryoidal shapes, of a white to gray, green, or brown color. See Note under Calamine.
smift: A match for firing a charge of powder, as in blasting; a fuse.
smoking: from Smoke. Smoking bean (Bot.), the long pod of the catalpa, or Indian-bean tree, often smoked by boys as a substitute for cigars. -- Smoking car, a railway car carriage reserved for the use of passengers who smoke tobacco.
smellless: Destitute of smell; having no odor. Daisies smell-less, yet most quaint. Beau & Fl.
smithery: 1. The workshop of a smith; a smithy or stithy. 2. Work done by a smith; smithing. The din of all his smithery may some time or other possibly wake this noble duke. Burke.
smeared: Having the color mark ings ill defined, as if rubbed; as, the smeared dagger moth (Apatela oblinita).
smotheriness: The quality or state of being smothery.
smelter: One who, or that which, smelts.
smatch: Taste; tincture; smack. (old) Thy life hath had some smatch of honor in it. Shak. | To smack. (old) Banister (1578).
smelt: 1. (Zoöl.) Any one of numerous species of small silvery salmonoid fishes of the genus Osmerus and allied genera, which ascend rivers to spawn, and sometimes become landlocked in lakes. | To melt or fuse, as, ore, for the purpose of separating and refining the metal; hence, to reduce; to refine; to flux or scorify; as, to smelt tin.
smother: 1. To destroy the life of by suffocation; to deprive of the air necessary for life; to cover up closely so as to prevent breathing; to suffocate; as, to smother a child. 2. | 1. To be suffocated or stifled. 2. To burn slowly, without sufficient air; to smolder.
smokeless: Making or having no smoke. "Smokeless towers." Pope.
smellfeast: 1. One who is apt to find and frequent good tables; a parasite; a sponger. The epicure and the smell-feast. South. 2. A feast at which the guests are supposed to feed upon the odors only of the viands.
smoldry: Smoldering; suffocating; smothery. (old) A flaming fire ymixt with smoldry smoke. Spenser.
smasher: 1. One who, or that which, smashes or breaks things to pieces. 2. Anything very large or extraordinary. [Slang] 3. One who passes counterfeit coin. [Cant, Eng.]
smithy: The workshop of a smith, esp. a blacksmith; a smithery; a stithy. [Written also smiddy.] Under a spreading chestnut tree The village smithy stands. Lonfellow.
smutty: 1. Soiled with smut; smutted. 2. Tainted with mildew; as, smutty corn. 3. Obscene; not modest or pure; as, a smutty saying. The smutty joke, ridiculously lewd. Smollett. -- Smut"ti*ly, adv. -- Smut"ti*ness, n.
smerk: Smart; jaunty; spruce. See Smirk, a. (old) So smerk, so smooth, his pricked ears. Spenser.
smelling: 1. The act of one who smells. 2. The sense by which odors are perceived; the sense of smell. Locke. Smelling bottle, a small bottle filled with something suited to stimulate the sense of smell, or to remove faintness, as spirits of ammonia.
smite: 1. To strike; to inflict a blow upon with the hand, or with any instrument held in the hand, or with a missile thrown by the hand; as, to smite with the fist, with a rod, sword, spear, or stone. | To strike; to collide; to beat. (old) The heart meleth, and the knees smite together. Nah. ii. 10.
smeary: Tending to smear or soil; adhesive; viscous. Rowe.
smellingsalts: An aromatic preparation of carbonate of ammonia and, often, some scent, to avoid or relieve faintness, headache, or the like.
